title: Present simple: habits and facts
explanation: Use the present simple for habits, routines and facts. Add -s or -es for he, she and it (she works, he watches). Use do/does for questions and negatives.
examples: I walk to work every day.
She works in a bank.
Does he like tea?
mistakes: Say 'He works', not 'He work'.
Say 'She doesn't like', not 'She doesn't likes'.

exercises.prompt: She ___ English every day.
He ___ (watch) TV in the evening.
Correct the sentence: He don't like coffee.
Order the words.

title: Prepositions of time: at, on, in
explanation: Use 'at' for clock times (at 5 o'clock), 'on' for days and dates (on Monday, on 3 May), and 'in' for months, years, seasons and parts of the day (in July, in 2020, in the morning).
examples: The class starts at nine.
We meet on Friday.
I was born in March.
mistakes: Say 'on Monday', not 'in Monday'.
Say 'at night', not 'in the night' for general time.

exercises.prompt: My birthday is ___ June.
The film starts ___ 8 o'clock.
Correct the sentence: I will see you in Saturday.
exercises.answer: I will see you on Saturday.

exercises.prompt: Order the words.

title: Present continuous vs present simple
explanation: Use the present continuous (am/is/are + -ing) for actions happening now or temporary situations. Use the present simple for habits. State verbs such as know, like and want are not normally used in the continuous.
examples: I am cooking dinner now.
She usually walks, but today she is taking the bus.
I know the answer.
mistakes: Say 'I know', not 'I am knowing'.
Say 'He is working', not 'He working'.

exercises.prompt: Please be quiet. The baby ___.
Look! It ___ (rain).
Correct the sentence: I am wanting a coffee.
Order the words.

title: Modals of obligation: must, have to, should
explanation: Use 'must' and 'have to' for strong obligation, 'should' for advice, and 'mustn't' for prohibition. 'Don't have to' means it is not necessary.
examples: You must wear a seatbelt.
I have to work tomorrow.
You should see a doctor.
mistakes: 'Mustn't' and 'don't have to' are different: one is forbidden, the other is optional.
Say 'must go', not 'must to go'.

exercises.prompt: You ___ park here. It is forbidden.
Tomorrow is a holiday, so you ___ (not / have to) work.
Correct the sentence: You must to wear a helmet.
Order the words.

title: Relative clauses: who, which, that, whose
explanation: Use 'who' for people, 'which' for things, 'that' for either in defining clauses, and 'whose' for possession. Non-defining clauses add extra information, use commas, and cannot use 'that'.
examples: The man who lives next door is a doctor.
This is the book that I told you about.
My sister, who lives in Leeds, is a nurse.
mistakes: Do not repeat the subject: 'The man who he called' is wrong.
Say 'the woman whose car was stolen', not 'who her car'.

exercises.prompt: The woman ___ car was stolen called the police.
The phone ___ I bought is broken. (which/that)
Correct the sentence: The man who he called me is my uncle.
exercises.answer: The man who called me is my uncle.

exercises.prompt: Order the words.

title: Used to and would for past habits
explanation: Use 'used to + verb' for past habits and states that are no longer true. 'Would' can describe repeated past actions but not states. 'Be used to + -ing' means being accustomed.
examples: I used to smoke, but I stopped.
We would visit our grandparents every summer.
I am used to getting up early.
mistakes: Say 'I didn't use to', not 'I didn't used to'.
Do not use 'would' for states: 'I used to have a dog'.

exercises.prompt: She ___ live in Paris, but now she lives in Rome.
I didn't ___ to like fish.
Correct the sentence: I am used to wake up early.
exercises.answer: I am used to waking up early.

exercises.prompt: Order the words.

title: Future forms: will, going to, present continuous
explanation: Use 'going to' for plans and predictions from evidence, 'will' for spontaneous decisions and promises, and the present continuous for fixed arrangements.
examples: I'm going to study medicine.
It's cold; I'll close the window.
We're meeting Anna at six.
mistakes: Do not use 'will' after 'if' for the condition: 'If it rains', not 'If it will rain'.
Say 'I'm meeting', not 'I meet' for arrangements.

exercises.prompt: The phone is ringing. I ___ answer it.
Look at those clouds! It ___ (rain).
Correct the sentence: If it will rain, we will stay home.
exercises.answer: If it rains, we will stay home.

exercises.prompt: Order the words.

title: Gerunds and infinitives
explanation: Some verbs take -ing (enjoy, avoid, suggest), some take to + verb (want, decide, hope), and some change meaning (stop doing vs stop to do; remember doing vs remember to do).
examples: I enjoy swimming.
She decided to leave.
He stopped smoking.
mistakes: Say 'I suggest going', not 'I suggest to go'.
Say 'I want to go', not 'I want going'.

exercises.prompt: She avoided ___ the question.
We decided ___ (move) to London.
Correct the sentence: He suggested to take a taxi.
Order the words.
exercises.explain: forgot + to-infinitive = did not do it.

title: Mixed conditionals
explanation: A mixed conditional links a past condition to a present result (if + past perfect, would + base verb) or a present condition to a past result (if + past simple, would have + past participle).
examples: If I had studied harder, I would be a doctor now.
If she were more careful, she would not have broken it.
If we had left earlier, we would be there already.
mistakes: Do not use 'would' in the if-clause.
Keep the tense pattern: past perfect then would.

exercises.prompt: If I ___ the job, I would be living in Dubai now.
If he had listened, he ___ (not / be) in trouble now.
Correct the sentence: If I would have money, I would buy it.
exercises.answer: If I had money, I would buy it.

exercises.prompt: Order the words.

title: Participle clauses
explanation: Participle clauses shorten sentences with the same subject: present participle for simultaneous or causal actions (Walking home, I met Tom), past participle for passive meaning (Seen from above, the city looks small), perfect participle for an earlier action (Having finished, she left).
examples: Walking down the street, I saw an old friend.
Having finished the report, she went home.
Built in 1900, the bridge is still used.
mistakes: The subject of the participle must be the subject of the main clause.
Avoid dangling participles: 'Walking home, the rain started' is wrong.

exercises.prompt: ___ the email, he closed his laptop.
___ (live) abroad for years, she speaks three languages.
Correct the sentence: Walking home, the rain started.
exercises.answer: Walking home, I got caught in the rain.

title: Nominalisation in formal writing
explanation: Nominalisation turns verbs and adjectives into nouns to make writing more formal and dense: 'They decided' becomes 'Their decision', 'It increased quickly' becomes 'a rapid increase'. Use it carefully: too much makes writing heavy.
examples: The rapid growth of cities has created pressure on housing.
Their failure to respond caused delay.
The introduction of the law led to a reduction in crime.
mistakes: Overuse makes sentences abstract and hard to read.
Check that the noun keeps the original meaning.

exercises.prompt: Formal version of "Prices rose sharply":
Complete: They decided quickly → Their quick ___ surprised us.
Correct the sentence: The country developed fast, which caused many problems.
exercises.answer: The rapid development of the country caused many problems.
